Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Oh, yes... she has trouble seeing the board in class, even when she sits right up front. Her teacher says she often squints and rubs her eyes during lessons. I'm worried it might affect her learning.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Actually, she likes the TV volume really loud. I've caught her turning it up to full blast sometimes, and I have to remind her to turn it down. Maybe her hearing is more sensitive than usual?

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: She complains about tooth sensitivity, especially with cold foods like ice cream or frozen yogurts. It makes her uncomfortable and she avoids those foods now.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Yes... the cardiologist found a valve issue in her heart. We go for regular check-ups to monitor it, and so far, everything seems under control. But I do get anxious about it.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: As a baby, she was slower to sit, stand, and walk compared to other kids. The pediatrician said it was just a developmental delay, but I worry it could be something more.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Feeding has been a challenge since birth. She has difficulty swallowing certain textures and often gags on her food. We've had to work with her to make mealtime less stressful.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: She has patal abnormalities that the specialists are monitoring. Also, her back has a bit of a curve, which the orthopedic doctor is keeping an eye on. These concerns keep me up at night, worrying about her future.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The cardiologist found a valve issue in the patient's heart, requiring regular check-ups to monitor it. Everything seems under control, but the parent gets anxious about it.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty swallowing certain textures and often gags on her food, making mealtime stressful. They have worked with her to make mealtime less stressful.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have swallowing difficulties, leading to challenges in eating and drinking.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experienced a developmental delay, particularly in sitting, standing, and walking, compared to other kids. The pediatrician said it was just a developmental delay, but the parent worries it could be something more.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has palatal abnormalities that the specialists are monitoring, and her back has a bit of a curve, prompting concern about her future.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have palatal abnormalities, and around 38% have heart conditions.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has palatal abnormalities that the specialists are monitoring, and her back has a bit of a curve, prompting concern about her future.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have palatal abnormalities.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences tooth sensitivity, especially with cold foods, making her uncomfortable and avoiding those foods now.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have tooth sensitivity.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school. The extra demands of mainstream secondary school may prove too challenging, and children may transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have swallowing difficulties, leading to challenges in eating and drinking.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, or anxiety. Medication(s) may be appropriate in some circumstances.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have behavioral differences.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis). Babies may experience a delayed closure of the soft spot on their head (anterior fontanelle). Many people with KBG syndrome have short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curvature of the 5th fingers (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient has tooth sensitivity, especially with cold foods, making her uncomfortable and avoiding those foods now.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: The patient has hearing concerns, and hearing should be carefully and regularly checked during the first few years.
c) Eyesight (ophthalmology) review: The patient has palatal abnormalities that the specialists are monitoring, and her back has a bit of a curve, prompting concern about her future.
d) Check position of testes in boys: The patient has undescended testes, and treatment can include bringing the testes down and fixing them in the scrotum with a simple surgical operation (orchidopexy).
e) Consider a palate review: The patient has palatal abnormalities that the specialists are monitoring, and her back has a bit of a curve, prompting concern about her future.
f) Referral for a cardiac review (including echo and ECG): The patient has a valve issue in her heart, requiring regular check-ups to monitor it.
g) If nothing is found (or already done) this does not need to be repeated: The patient has a valve issue in her heart, requiring regular check-ups to monitor it.
h) Consider a skeletal review (X-ray of the wrist (to determine bone age), hip, spine and skull): The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis).
i) Any concerns around asymmetric hip creases in infancy and/or asymmetric or painful gait should prompt medical review: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis).
j) Consider review and investigation for tethered cord (MRI) where clinical concerns arise on an individual basis (especially if sacral dimple is present): The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis).
k) Monitor growth velocity: If height is below the 2nd centile, consider referral for endocrine investigations on an individual basis and within context of familial heights.
l) Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and behavioural therapy: The patient has palatal abnormalities that the specialists are monitoring, and her back has a bit of a curve, prompting concern about her future.

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The vast majority of people with KBG syndrome do not have a very serious heart condition. However, a study of 40 European patients showed that 15/40 (38%) had heart conditions. These included changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few required surgery, but some just needed monitoring.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The vast majority of people with KBG syndrome learn to speak but speech delay is very common. Hearing loss and subtle palate problems can worsen speech delay. Differences in the pitch and quality of the voice can also be observed.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The vast majority of people with KBG syndrome have hypotonia, low muscle tone. The physiotherapist says it's why he has trouble with certain movements and balance. They are working on exercises to help strengthen his muscles.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: His teeth break or chip so easily! We have to be super careful what he eats and make sure he brushes them just right.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: While most do not have very significant anomalies of the roof of the mouth (palate), a proportion have subtler anomalies. These can affect speech development and feeding, meaning referral for specialist review may be appropriate in some cases.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: Poor thing... his teeth break or chip so easily! We have to be super careful what he eats and make sure he brushes them just right.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The vast majority of people with KBG syndrome need extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school. The extra demands of mainstream secondary school may prove too challenging, and children may transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP). Those with chromosome deletions may have more significant problems, which are probably related to other genes which are also deleted.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: He has hypotonia, low muscle tone. The physiotherapist says it's why he has trouble with certain movements and balance. They are working on exercises to help strengthen his muscles.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: Some people with KBG syndrome have an unusual structure of their spinal bones which can give rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis). Babies may experience a delayed closure of the soft spot on their head (anterior fontanelle). Many people with KBG syndrome have short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curvature of the 5th fingers (clinodactyly). A small number of children have had hip dysplasia, in which the hip joints are easily dislocated.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

a) Regular dental check-ups.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5 (even if earlier reviews give a clear response).
c) Eyesight (ophthalmology) review.

e) Consider a palate review (particularly if there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns).
f) Referral for a cardiac review (including echo and ECG) following diagnosis.
g) If nothing is found (or already done) this does not need to be repeated.
h) Consider a skeletal review (X-ray of the wrist (to determine bone age), hip, spine and skull) in children following diagnosis.
i) Any concerns around asymmetric hip creases in infancy and/or asymmetric or painful gait should prompt medical review.
j) Consider review and investigation for tethered cord (MRI) where clinical concerns arise on an individual basis (especially if sacral dimple is present).
k) Monitor growth velocity: if height is below the 2nd centile consider referral for endocrine investigations on an individual basis and within context of familial heights.
l) Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and behavioral therapy.

a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a triangular-shaped face, wide-spaced eyes, and thick eyebrows that sometimes join in the center (synophrys). She also has short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curved 5th finger (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems such as astigmatism (the front of the eye is not perfectly rounded, causing blurry vision), and short- or long-sightedness (myopia and hypermetropia). Squint (strabismus), where the eyes do not look in the same direction, can occasionally be a feature. Treatment can include patching, exercises, glasses, and surgery to bring the eyes into line.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

a) How this affects the patient: The patient complains about tooth sensitivity when eating cold foods like ice cream or yogurt. It has been going on for a while now.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school. b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety. Medication(s) may be appropriate in some circumstances.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of her spinal bones, which can lead to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis). Babies may experience a delayed closure of the soft spot on their head (anterior fontanelle). Many people with KBG syndrome have short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curvature of the 5th finger (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome are reported to have seizures, of varying types. Seizures typically respond to the usual antiepileptic treatments. In a small number of cases, epilepsy can be difficult to treat.
